desc: The civilian organisation Ryan Graves founded in 2022 to build the reporting channel the Navy did not provide. Its existence is the most concrete measure of the failure documented in Graves's own testimony: after his squadron's near-midair in Warning Area W-72, 'there was no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings,' so an aircrew nonprofit now performs an intake function that belongs to the Naval Safety Command and the FAA. By July 2023 Graves told Congress it had 'nearly 5,000 members' and was 'actively working with more than 30 UAP witnesses who have approached us.' The organisation's programme sits squarely on the recommendations the NASA UAP Independent Study Team published on 14 September 2023 - enhancing the Aviation Safety Reporting System for commercial pilot UAP reporting and working with the FAA on civilian pilot procedures - recommendations Mike Gold pressed again in House Oversight testimony on 13 November 2024. The organisation is a witness-chain hub: it is where aircrew who will not report inside the chain of command go instead, which makes it both an evidentiary asset and a symptom.

claims.text: Americans for Safe Aerospace is a military pilot-led 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded by Ryan Graves, a former U.S. Navy lieutenant and F/A-18 pilot, headquartered at 1620 I St NW Suite 900, Washington, DC 20006; Graves is Founder and Executive Director.

As of 2026 ASA publicly reports more than 30,000 members and describes itself as 'the world's largest UAP advocacy community dedicated to pilot support, aerospace safety, data-driven research, and analysis of UAP.'

At launch of its UAP Witness Campaign on July 18, 2023, ASA stated that 'More than 30 commercial aircrew and military witnesses have already approached ASA to share their accounts' and that the organization had more than 4,000 members.

In written testimony to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs on July 26, 2023, Graves stated ASA had 'nearly 5,000 members' and was 'actively working with more than 30 UAP witnesses who have approached us.'

Graves testified that ASA advisor Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, former head of NOAA and Oceanographer of the Navy, received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 while serving with Fleet Forces Command, titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue', attaching the GO FAST video and citing multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP off Virginia Beach; the email was removed from Gallaudet's system and his deputy's the next day and was never discussed, and Gallaudet 'presumes the email was removed in connection with a classified special access program.'

Graves testified to the W-72 incident: two F/A-18s entering Warning Area W-72 ten miles east of Virginia Beach through a single GPS entry point, one hundred feet apart, when a pilot saw 'a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere, motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point'; the jets took evasive action, terminated the mission, and the squadron's safety report received no official acknowledgement and no further reporting mechanism.
Graves testified that the UAP Task Force reported in 2021 that there were 11 near misses with UAP, citing the ODNI Preliminary Assessment on UAP dated June 25, 2021.

Graves testified that in April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operation managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP.

ASA's national security advisory bench includes Jay Stratton (former Director, UAP Task Force), Christopher Mellon (former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence), Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet (former head of NOAA), and Kirk McConnell (former professional staff, Senate Armed Services Committee).

ASA's aircrew leadership includes David Fravor and Alex Dietrich, the first former Navy pilots to meet with Congress about their UAP encounter, plus Michael Greene (former U.S. Marines F/A-18 weapons system officer) and Sam Fletcher (former U.S. Navy F/A-18 weapons system officer).

ASA's policy and science advisors include Susan McCue (former chief of staff to Senator Harry Reid), Bryan Bender (former defense editor, Politico), Mike Gold (former NASA UAP Independent Study Team member), David Radzanowski (former CFO and Chief of Staff, NASA), Avi Loeb (Harvard), Garry Nolan (Stanford), Robin Hanson (George Mason) and Ravi Starzl (Carnegie Mellon).

ASA's witness process is witness-controlled: confidential outline, ASA interview, evaluation with a subject-matter advisor, then referral to congressional staff, Members, or AARO 'only at the explicit permission and willingness of the UAP witness.'

ASA endorsed the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 (118th Congress), which would allow civilian pilots to report UAP through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System, provide protection against retaliation, and make all UAP reports publicly available; the mechanism was recommended by the NASA UAP Independent Study Team.

ASA documented that the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 was proposed by Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, and that its key mechanism was a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to 'hold hearings, administer oaths, and subpoena [UAP] witnesses and documents' in connection with declassifying UAP documents for public distribution.

dossier.denialPosture: ASA does not deny; it documents. Its posture toward the government's own position is captured in Graves's testimony noting that AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick told Congress he operated only under Title 10 authority and needed Title 50 authorities and access to scientifically calibrated intelligence-community sensors, then indicated in his first public interview a week before the hearing that he had what he needed, a reversal Graves flagged on the record as unexplained.
dossier.narrative:
ASA's origin is a specific failure of the reporting system. Graves joined the Navy in 2009 and by 2014 was flying with VFA-11 near Virginia Beach when a radar upgrade began producing unknown tracks that were initially dismissed as software glitches and then corroborated on infrared, confirming their physical presence. The sightings became routine enough to appear in daily briefs. The pivotal event was in Warning Area W-72, an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach where all traffic enters through a single GPS point at a set altitude. As two jets crossed the threshold one hundred feet apart, one pilot saw a dark gray cube inside a clear sphere, motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point. Both aircraft took evasive action and terminated the mission. The squadron filed a safety report. There was no official acknowledgement and no mechanism to report further sightings. Graves founded ASA to build the mechanism that did not exist.

The organization scaled faster than anyone planned. Its July 18, 2023 launch release for the UAP Witness Campaign stated that more than 30 commercial aircrew and military witnesses had already approached it and that ASA had more than 4,000 members. Eight days later, in written testimony to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, Graves reported nearly 5,000 members and more than 30 UAP witnesses being actively worked. By 2026 the public membership figure is over 30,000. The witness profile is itself a finding: the majority are commercial pilots at major airlines, often veterans with decades of experience, and their reports frequently open with an apology, in Graves's phrasing, 'I apologize, I realize this will sound crazy.' They describe objects at altitudes apparently above 40,000 feet, potentially in low earth orbit or in the grey zone below the Karman line, executing right-hand turns, retrograde orbits and j-hooks, with recurring clusters north of Hawaii and in the North Atlantic. They are adamant these are not Starlink flares.

ASA's process is deliberately witness-controlled. A pilot or veteran contacts the organization confidentially with an outline, ASA conducts an interview, brings in an advisor with relevant expertise for evaluation, and only then, and only with the witness's explicit permission, are next steps taken, which can include meetings with congressional staff and Members or with AARO. Most witnesses do not want to speak publicly and fear professional consequences; they want their account added to the data set. That design is a direct response to the retaliation problem that runs through the whole file.

The advisory bench is what makes ASA structurally significant rather than merely large. Its pilots include David Fravor and Alex Dietrich, the first former Navy pilots to meet with Congress about their UAP encounter, plus Michael Greene and Sam Fletcher. Its national security advisors are Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force, Christopher Mellon, Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff on the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is the committee that wrote the AARO statutes and whose chair and ranking member sit inside the twelve-member waived-SAP notification group. Its policy advisors include Susan McCue, former chief of staff to Senator Harry Reid, and Bryan Bender, former defense editor at Politico, plus Mike Gold of the NASA UAP Independent Study Team and David Radzanowski, former CFO and Chief of Staff at NASA. Its science bench includes Avi Loeb of Harvard, Garry Nolan of Stanford, Robin Hanson of George Mason and Ravi Starzl of Carnegie Mellon.

The single most operationally important thing ASA has put on the congressional record came through Gallaudet. Graves testified that while serving as an Admiral with Fleet Forces Command, Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 from the Operations Commander to all one- and two-star subordinates, titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue', attaching the GO FAST video and raising concerns about multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP in the early warning area off Virginia Beach, with a note that the exercise might be shut down for safety reasons. Gallaudet reviewed it with his deputy. The next day the email was removed from both of their systems, and despite routine in-person meetings with that group, no one ever discussed it again. Gallaudet's stated presumption is that the removal was connected to a classified special access program. That is a flag officer, on the record through a congressional witness, describing the retroactive deletion of a safety-of-flight communication.

Graves also entered two hard data points into the House record: that the UAP Task Force reported in 2021 there had been eleven near misses with UAP, citing the ODNI Preliminary Assessment of June 25, 2021, and that in April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operations managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP. He also flagged an unexplained reversal by AARO's director, who told Congress he operated only under Title 10 authority and needed Title 50 authorities and access to scientifically calibrated intelligence-community sensors, then indicated in his first public interview shortly before the hearing that he had what he needed.

On policy, ASA endorsed the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 in the 118th Congress, which would let civilian pilots report through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System with anti-retaliation protection and public release of all reports, a mechanism recommended by the NASA UAP Independent Study Team. ASA's July 2023 release also documents the organization's read of the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023, sponsored by Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, whose central mechanism was a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to hold hearings, administer oaths, and subpoena UAP witnesses and documents.

dossier.whatItIs: Americans for Safe Aerospace (ASA) is a military pilot-led 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2023 by Ryan Graves, a former U.S. Navy F/A-18F pilot from strike fighter squadron VFA-11. It operates a confidential intake channel through which military and commercial aircrew report UAP encounters, and it functions as the principal non-governmental witness pipeline into Congress. Headquartered at 1620 I St NW Suite 900, Washington, DC, it describes itself as the world's largest UAP advocacy community and reported more than 30,000 members as of 2026, up from roughly 4,000 at its founding.
dossier.whyImplicated: ASA is the institution that solved the collection problem the government created. Because there is no protected, non-stigmatizing reporting route for commercial pilots, and because military witnesses face a confusing internal process, the observational data that would test the phenomenon has never been aggregated by the state. ASA aggregates it privately and then feeds it to Congress, which is why its founder's July 2023 testimony landed as the first public congressional hearing to take military pilot and whistleblower evidence. More importantly for a concealment map, ASA is where several people who were inside the classified system have landed: Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force; Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence; Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, former head of NOAA and Oceanographer of the Navy; and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. That roster means ASA holds institutional memory of both the task force that collected the data and the committee staff that wrote the oversight statutes. It is a private organization staffed with the government's own former custodians.
